Entry economics are deteriorating faster than demand is growing in most jurisdictions except South Africa and Nigeria.

verdict: Côte d'Ivoire is a fast-growing (~XOF 706bn / ~$1.26bn licensed-sector turnover in 2024, +20.5% YoY) but structurally closed market: every online vertical – sports betting, online casino, virtuals – sits inside LONACI's exclusive State concession, and the 17 private brands on the ARJH register (up from 3 in Dec 2023) trade only as LONACI agrément-holders. September 2026 crystallised the tension in that model: national search demand rose 21.7% MoM and 12.6% YoY, Betclic took 55.2% of it, and the concessionaire's own online brand slipped to 6%. For an entrant the question is not 'can we get a licence' but 'can we secure a LONACI agrément on economics that survive a 5% online tax, 30% corporate tax, a 7.5% player-winnings withholding and a regulator that is visibly hardening enforcement (USSJH decree, April 2026).'

verdict: Latin America in 2026 is no longer one growth story. Brazil — the region's largest regulated market at BRL 37bn (~$7.1bn) GGR in 2025 and BRL 20.07bn (~$3.9bn, +15% YoY) in H1-26 — has been switched off by Provisional Measure 1.394/2026 since 6 October, and Lula's re-election on 25 October removes the quickest political route back. The five remaining markets now diverge on maturity rather than size: Colombia (regulated since 2016, 21 online operators, online VAT struck down in April), Peru (cleanest framework, but ISC-on-stakes risk of 1%→5%), Mexico (scale under a 1947 law with a 50% headline IEPS), Argentina (~50% offshore, acquisition-only entry) and Chile (bill still in Congress, framework 2027-28 at best).
